result:
Neither five nor ten. The premise is the problem: more agents don't always give better results.

Here's a concrete case from Anthropic's engineering team. They built a multi-agent research system, and it beat a single agent by about 90% on their internal test. But it used about 15× the tokens of a normal chat, and a single agent already uses about 4×. They say much of the gain came from spending more tokens, not from the agent count itself. Splitting work also pays off mainly for tasks that break into independent, parallel pieces. They say tasks where agents must share the same context, or depend heavily on each other, are a poor fit.

Now apply that to your makerspace assistant. A typical request looks like this: "Can I use the laser cutter Thursday, and what settings for 3mm acrylic?" The steps depend on each other: check the training status, look up the manual, check the calendar, then book. That's sequential and shares context. Splitting it across ten agents would add handoffs and token cost, and your budget is small.

Start with one agent with good tools, and make fixed workflow steps wherever the path is predictable. Add a second agent only when you can name a job that is parallel and independent, and you can show the single agent fails at it.

Quick check: which part of the assistant is the most parallel and independent, and which is the most sequential?

I can turn this into a lesson on workflows versus agents versus multi-agent systems, which is the heart of your design-review argument. Want one?

Sources:
- [Anthropic Engineering: How we built our multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- [Simon Willison's summary](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/14/multi-agent-research-system/)

I only got the figures from a search summary, not the full post, so check them there before quoting them at your review.
